claims.source: Zebrafish scRNAseq data show that both cib2 and cib3 are expressed in the inner ear while primarily cib2 is expressed in lateral-line hair cells (Baek et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior scRNAseq studies.

claims.claim: The probability of a startle response was significantly reduced in cib2 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: We found that, compared to controls, the probability of a startle response was significantly reduced in cib2 mutants (Figure 5A, control: 0.71 ± 0.04; cib2: 0.28 ± 0.06, p=0.005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: cib3 mutant zebrafish startle with a similar frequency compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast, cib3 mutants startle with a similar frequency compared to controls (Figure 5A, p=0.36).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish exhibited a complete absence of startle responses.
claims.source: In cib2;cib3 mutant animals we observed a complete absence of startle responses (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish exhibited spontaneous circling behavior.
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed that cib2;cib3 mutants but not cib2 or cib3 mutants exhibited spontaneous circling behavior, an additional indicator of inner ear dysfunction in zebrafish (Nicolson et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observational data and a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal acoustic startle responses in zebrafish.
claims.source: Together our behavioral results indicate that Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal acoustic startle responses in zebrafish.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined acoustic startle response data from zebrafish mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of Cib2, but not Cib3, can impair auditory function in zebrafish.
claims.source: Furthermore, just loss of Cib2, but not Cib3 can impair auditory function in zebrafish.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the acoustic startle response data showing reduced responses in cib2 mutants but not cib3 mutants.

claims.claim: The percent of hair cells per neuromast labeling with FM 1-43 was significantly reduced in cib2 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: We found that, compared to controls, the percent of hair cells per neuromast labeling with FM 1–43 was significantly reduced in cib2 mutants (Figure 5B, D and E, control: 97.6 ± 1.2; cib2: 37.5 ± 6.9, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E.

claims.claim: A similar percent of hair cells per neuromast labeled with FM 1-43 in cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast, a similar percent of hair cells per neuromast labeled with FM 1–43 in cib3 mutants, compared to controls (Figure 5B, D and F, cib3: 95.7 ± 1.9, p=1.0).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and F.

claims.claim: The average FM 1-43 label was reduced in cib2 but not cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: We found that, compared to controls, the average FM 1–43 label was reduced in cib2 but not cib3 mutants (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 intensity quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish, there was a complete absence of FM 1-43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells.
claims.source: In cib2;cib3 mutant animals we observed a complete absence of FM 1–43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells (Figure 5B, D and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and G.

claims.claim: Both Cib2 and Cib3 are needed to ensure normal MET in all lateral-line hair cells in zebrafish.
claims.source: Thus, taken together the results of our FM 1–43 labeling analysis are consistent with a requirement for both Cib2 and Cib3 to ensure normal MET in all lateral-line hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined FM 1-43 labeling data from zebrafish mutants.

claims.claim: Significantly fewer cells were mechanosensitive in cib2 and cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: We quantified the number of hair bundles per neuromast with mechanosensitive Ca2+ responses, and found that compared to controls, significantly fewer cells were mechanosensitive in cib2 and cib2;cib3 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, control: 92.2 ± 2.5; cib2: 49.9 ± 5.8, cib2;cib3: 19.0 ± 6.6, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: In cib3 mutant zebrafish, the percent of mechanosensitive cells per neuromast was similar compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast, in cib3 mutants, the percent of mechanosensitive cells per neuromast was similar compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, cib3: 94.5 ± 1.8, p=1.0).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The magnitude of mechanosensitive Ca2+ responses in cib2 and cib2;cib3 hair bundles were significantly reduced compared to controls.
claims.source: This quantification revealed that, while cib3 mechanosensitive responses were not different compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C, GCaMP6s % ∆F/F control: 70.6±5.9; cib3: 71.6±5.2, p>1.0), the magnitude of responses in cib2 and cib2;cib3 hair bundles were significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C, GCaMP6s % ∆F/F control: 70.6 ± 5.9; cib2: 33.0 ± 5.8, cib2;cib3: 14.7 ± 1.9, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: Loss of Cib2 alone, but not Cib3, can impair mechanosensory function in the majority of zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
claims.source: Overall, our in vivo FM 1–43 and Ca2+-imaging analyses revealed that loss of Cib2 alone, but not Cib3 can impair mechanosensory function in the majority of zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined FM 1-43 and calcium imaging data from zebrafish mutants.

claims.claim: Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal MET function in all lateral-line hair cells in zebrafish.
claims.source: Furthermore, Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal MET function in all lateral-line hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined functional data from zebrafish mutants.

claims.claim: In the zebrafish pLL, hair cells that detect posterior flow rely on Tmc2b, while hair cells that detect anterior flow rely on both Tmc2b and Tmc2a.
claims.source: In the primary posterior lateral line (pLL) hair cells are oriented to respond to either anterior or posterior fluid flow. The subset of hair cells that detects posterior flow relies on Tmc2b while the subset that detects anterior flow relies on both Tmc2b and Tmc2a (Figure 6A; Chou et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the zebrafish crista, short cells rely on Tmc2a, while tall cells rely on either Tmc1 or Tmc2b for mechanosensitive function.
claims.source: Short cells rely on Tmc2a, while tall cells rely on either Tmc1 or Tmc2b for mechanosensitive function (Figure 6E; Smith et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: In cib2 mutant zebrafish, significantly more of the FM 1-43 positive hair cells in the pLL were oriented to respond to posterior flow.
claims.source: In contrast, when we examined cib2 mutants, we found that significantly more of the FM 1–43 positive hair cells were oriented to respond to posterior flow (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 FX labeling and hair bundle orientation analysis shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: In cib2 mutant zebrafish, the residual Cib3 present in pLL hair cells preferentially functions in hair cells that express primarily Tmc2b and are oriented to respond to posterior flow.
claims.source: This indicates that in cib2 mutants, the residual Cib3 present in pLL hair cells preferentially functions in hair cells that express primarily Tmc2b and are oriented to respond to posterior flow (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the hair cell orientation data in cib2 mutants and known Tmc expression patterns.

claims.claim: Cib2 can function with hair cells that express Tmc2b as well as hair cells that express Tmc2b and Tmc2a.
claims.source: On the other hand, Cib2 can function with hair cells that express Tmc2b (respond to posterior flow) as well as hair cells that express Tmc2b and Tmc2a (respond to anterior flow).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the hair cell orientation data in cib2 mutants and known Tmc expression patterns.

claims.claim: No hair cells in the medial cristae were FM 4-64 positive in cib2;cib3 double mutant zebrafish.
claims.source: We found that similar to our FM 1–43 results in the pLL, no hair cells in the medial cristae were FM 4–64 positive in cib2;cib3 double mutants (Figure 6I–I').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6I-I'.

claims.claim: There were no defects in FM 4-64 labeling in the crista of cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
claims.source: In addition, similar to the pLL we observed no defects in FM 4–64 labeling in the crista of cib3 mutants compared to controls (Figure 6G–G').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6G-G'.

claims.claim: Short hair cells in the crista of cib2 mutant zebrafish failed to label with FM 4-64.
claims.source: Interestingly we found that short hair cells in the crista of cib2 mutants failed to label with FM 4–64 (Figure 6H–H').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6H-H'.

claims.claim: Cib2 is required for mechanosensitive function in hair cells that express Tmc2a in zebrafish.
claims.source: Overall, our functional assessment of MET based on hair cell subtypes within the zebrafish pLL and inner ear suggests that Cib2 is required for mechanosensitive function in hair cells that express Tmc2a.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined functional data from different hair cell subtypes in zebrafish.

claims.claim: The AF2 model of TMC1 alone resembles previous TMEM16/OSCA-based models of TMC1.
claims.source: The AF2 model of TMC1 alone resembles previous TMEM16/OSCA-based models of TMC1 and is also consistent with a recent cryo-EM structure of the worm TMC-1 protein (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies and represents a comparison of models.

claims.claim: TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10).
claims.source: In these models, TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1) and a putative pore is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer (Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021), away from the dimeric interface involving α10.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: A putative pore in TMC1 is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer.
claims.source: In these models, TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1) and a putative pore is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer (Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021), away from the dimeric interface involving α10.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: AF2 models of TMC1 feature an additional amphipathic helix, denoted α0, extending almost parallel to the expected plane of the membrane bilayer.
claims.source: Our new models feature an additional amphipathic helix, which we denote α0, extending almost parallel to the expected plane of the membrane bilayer without crossing towards the extracellular side (as observed for a mostly hydrophobic α0 in OSCA channels and labeled as H3 in the worm TMC-1 structure) (Jeong et al., 2022; Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The intracellular domain linking helices α2 and α3 (IL1) adopts a helix-loop-helix fold.
claims.source: The intracellular domain linking helices α2 and α3, denoted here as IL1, adopts a helix-loop-helix with the two helices running parallel to each other and differing in length (Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4; Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1-4.

claims.claim: The IL1 fold is the same as observed in its crystal structure in complex with CIB3.
claims.source: This is the same fold observed in its crystal structure in complex with CIB3 (Liang et al., 2021), which validated the modeling approach.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural research and validates the modeling approach.

claims.claim: AF2 models of TMC1 in complex with CIB2 suggest that the N-terminus (NT) of TMC1 also interacts with CIB2.
claims.source: Interestingly, AF2 models of TMC1 in complex with CIB2 suggest that the N-terminus (NT) of TMC1 also interacts with CIB2 (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: In the AF2 model, CIB2 is clamped between TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1.
claims.source: In our model, CIB2 is clamped between TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 while the first helix of TMC1-IL1 runs parallel to the membrane plane interacting with the base of α1 and the intracellular linkers between α4 and α5, α6 and α7, and α8 and α9.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data and structural analysis.

claims.claim: The predicted interaction between TMC1-NT and CIB2 is consistent with previous biochemical data.
claims.source: Notably, the predicted interaction between TMC1-NT and CIB2 is consistent with previous biochemical data (Giese et al., 2017), while the overall model resolves seemingly contradictory results indicating that either the NT or IL1 of TMC1 was responsible for interactions with CIB proteins (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies and represents a reconciliation of previous findings.

claims.claim: AF2 models of TMC1 with CIB3 and of TMC2 with CIB2/3 predicted the same architecture for the TMC1/2 + CIB2/3 complexes where CIB proteins are clamped between the IL1 and NT domains of TMCs.
claims.source: Additional AF2 models of TMC1 with CIB3 and of TMC2 with CIB2/3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) predicted the same architecture for the TMC1/2 + CIB2/3 complexes where CIB proteins are clamped between the IL1 and NT domains of TMCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Predictions for fish TMC + CIB complexes show the same general architecture as mammalian complexes.
claims.source: Predictions for fish complexes also show the same general architecture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: NMR experiments validated the clamp model for Homo sapiens TMC + CIB interactions.
claims.source: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments were used to validate the clamp model for Homo sapiens (hs) TMC + CIB interactions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMR experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The addition of hs TMC1-NT induced additional chemical shift perturbations in [U-15N]-hs CIB2 + hs TMC1-IL1, demonstrating that TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT bind simultaneously to CIB2.
claims.source: Moreover, the addition of hs TMC1-NT induced additional chemical shift perturbations in many, but not all peaks, demonstrating that the TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT ligands bind simultaneously to [U-15N]-hs CIB2 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 6B.

claims.claim: Similar NMR results were observed for [U-15N]-hs CIB3 with TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT.
claims.source: We observed similar results when comparing spectra for [U-15N]-hs CIB3 alone, co-refolded with hs TMC1-IL1, and upon addition of hs TMC1-NT (Figure 7—figure supplement 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6C-D.

claims.claim: Direct heteromeric interactions between CIB2 and CIB3 are unlikely.
claims.source: A control experiment with the co-refolded mix of hs CIB3 + hs TMC1-IL1 and [U-15N]-hs CIB2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 6E) revealed no change in chemical shifts indicating that direct heteromeric interactions between CIB2 and CIB3 are unlikely.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMR control experiment data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6E.

claims.claim: NMR data strongly support a model in which human CIB2/3 proteins are clamped between TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT.
claims.source: Thus, taken together, the NMR data strongly support a model in which human CIB2/3 proteins are clamped between TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT as suggested by AF2 and consistent with prior biochemical data revealing interactions with either TMC1-NT or TMC1-IL1 (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined NMR data, AF2 modeling, and prior biochemical studies.

claims.claim: Equilibrium simulations of TMC1 and TMC2 alone revealed stable conformations for the transmembrane domains but a highly mobile NT domain.
claims.source: Equilibrium simulations of TMC1 and TMC2 alone revealed stable conformations for the transmembrane domains of these proteins, but a highly mobile NT domain (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In simulations where CIB2 or CIB3 were present, more stable conformations of N-termini along with stable salt bridges were observed.
claims.source: In simulations where CIB2 or CIB3 were present, with or without bound Ca2+, we observed more stable conformations of N-termini along with stable salt bridges (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: BSA analysis suggests that TMC1 and TMC2 have more contacts with CIB3 than with CIB2.
claims.source: Buried surface area (BSA) for the TMC + CIB complexes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, C and E, Figure 8—source data 2) revealed a possible trend in which TMC1 and TMC2 have more contacts with CIB3 than with CIB2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BSA analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Parts of the amphipathic α0 helices spontaneously partitioned at the membrane interface with their hydrophobic sides pointing toward the lipid bilayer core.
claims.source: Longer, Anton 2, 960-ns long equilibrium trajectories of TMC1 with CIB2 and bound Ca2+ in a mixed bilayer and TMC1 with CIB2 and (un)bound Ca2+ in a POPC bilayer revealed how parts of the amphipathic α0 helices spontaneously partitioned at the membrane interface with their hydrophobic sides pointing toward the lipid bilayer core (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of LHFPL5 has been shown to interact with the TMC1 amphipathic helix, which might be essential for channel function in mice.
claims.source: The N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of LHFPL5 has been shown to interact with this TMC1 amphipathic helix, which might be essential for channel function in mice (Qiu et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: In Anton 2 equilibrium trajectories, contacts between CIB2 and the TMC1-IL1 and -NT remained, confirming the stability of the complex over a microsecond timescale.
claims.source: Regardless, in all Anton 2 equilibrium trajectories contacts between CIB2 and the TMC1-IL1 and -NT remained, thus confirming the stability of the complex over a microsecond timescale.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In systems with pure POPC bilayers, permeation of K+ was observed in either one or both pores of the TMC1 dimer, with or without CIB2 or CIB3 and with or without bound Ca2+.
claims.source: In systems with pure POPC bilayers, we observed permeation of K+ in either one or both pores of the TMC1 dimer, with or without CIB2 or CIB3 and with or without bound Ca2+, despite the presence of Cl- (150 mM KCl).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data with applied voltage.

claims.claim: In all cases where a clear conductive state was monitored, almost exclusive passage of K+ was observed with conductance values that reached up to ~138 pS for a single pore.
claims.source: Variability of the conductance state was attributed to partial blockage by lipids and poor sampling, but in all cases in which a clear conductive state was monitored, we observed the almost exclusive passage of K+ with conductance values that reached up to ~138 pS for a single pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data with applied voltage.

claims.claim: The conductance values monitored in simulations are consistent with previous simulations and with the expected conductance of the inner-ear transduction channel.
claims.source: While simulations tend to overestimate bulk KCl conductivity and in some cases, predictions need to be scaled down (by a factor of ~0.6) (Walujkar et al., 2021), the conductance values monitored here are consistent with previous simulations and with the expected conductance of the inner-ear transduction channel (Beurg et al., 2021; Walujkar et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior simulation and experimental data.

claims.claim: Smaller conductance values were observed for TMC1 systems with mixed lipid bilayers compared to POPC bilayers.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed smaller conductance values for TMC1 systems with mixed lipid bilayers (at most ~22 pS for a single pore), regardless of the presence of CIB2 or CIB3, with or without bound Ca2+ (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: The reduced conductance values observed for mixed-membrane systems were attributed in part to pore blockage by cholesterol and lipids in the initial setup.
claims.source: The reduced conductance values observed for mixed-membrane systems were attributed in part to pore blockage by cholesterol and lipids in the initial setup.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of the simulation trajectories.

claims.claim: Anton 2 simulations revealed a trend in which TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound.
claims.source: Interestingly, Anton 2 simulations of TMC1, TMC1 + CIB2, and TMC1 + CIB2 + Ca2+ in pure POPC membranes subjected to –0.5 V, –0.25 V, and –0.125 V for 480 ns, 480 ns, and 960 ns, respectively, revealed a trend in which TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound (Figure 8E, Figure 8—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: The observation that TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound may explain why CIB2 is essential for normal TMC1 function.
claims.source: This may begin to explain why CIB2 is essential for normal TMC1 function.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the simulation data showing increased conductance with CIB2.

claims.claim: Simulations of TMC2 with an applied transmembrane voltage revealed a more closed state when compared to TMC1.
claims.source: Simulations of TMC2 with an applied transmembrane voltage of –0.5 V revealed a more closed state when compared to our TMC1 model, regardless of membrane composition and presence or absence of CIB2, CIB3, and bound Ca2+ (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The maximum conductance for TMC2 did not reach above ~64 pS, suggesting that the conformation simulated is less open than the ones explored in simulations of TMC1.
claims.source: Conduction of K+ was observed in most cases, but the maximum conductance did not reach above ~64 pS, suggesting that the conformation simulated is less open than the ones explored in simulations of TMC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the conductance values observed in TMC2 simulations.

claims.claim: TMC2 may have an intrinsic lower single-channel conductance than TMC1.
claims.source: We also speculate that this is due to TMC2 having an intrinsic lower single-channel conductance than TMC1, as has been suggested by some experiments (Kim et al., 2013), but not others (Pan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on simulation data and conflicting prior experimental results.

claims.claim: The TMC2 model may not be in a fully open conformation, which can only be reached upon mechanical stimulation.
claims.source: It is also possible that our TMC2 model is not in a fully open conformation, which can only be reached upon mechanical stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the limitations of the TMC2 model.

claims.claim: Simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels.
claims.source: Regardless, our simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels and that these proteins can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined molecular dynamics simulation data showing K+ permeation.

claims.claim: TMC1 and TMC2 can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
claims.source: Regardless, our simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels and that these proteins can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined molecular dynamics simulation data showing stable interactions.

claims.claim: CIB2 and CIB3 are important for stereocilia maintenance and MET in mouse vestibular hair cells.
claims.source: Recently, Wang et al., 2023 have suggested that CIB2 and CIB3 are important for stereocilia maintenance and MET in mouse vestibular hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claims.claim: Cib2 is highly expressed in the striolar region while Cib3 is expressed in the extrastriolar regions of mouse vestibular organs.
claims.source: This work demonstrated that similar to Tmc1 and Tmc2, Cib2 is highly expressed in the striolar region while Cib3 is expressed in the extrastriolar regions, and mice lacking both Cib2 and Cib3 had no MET and deficits in vestibular hair cell bundle structure (Wang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claims.claim: Vestibular hair cells in mice and zebrafish lacking CIB2 and CIB3 are not degenerated but have no detectable MET.
claims.source: We demonstrate that vestibular hair cells in mice and zebrafish lacking CIB2 and CIB3 are not degenerated but have no detectable MET, assessed via FM 1–43 dye uptake, at time points when MET function is well developed in wild-type hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claims.claim: A similar structural-function phenotype has been reported in auditory hair cells in Tmc1/Tmc2 double mutant mice.
claims.source: Similar structural-function phenotype has been reported in auditory hair cells in Tmc1/Tmc2 double mutant mice (Kawashima et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The study provides strong genetic evidence for the direct functional relationship between CIB and TMC proteins in regulating MET both in auditory and vestibular hair cells.
claims.source: Besides the known in vitro interactions (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021), our study provides strong genetic evidence for the direct functional relationship between CIB and TMC proteins in regulating MET both in auditory and vestibular hair cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined genetic and functional data from the current study.

claims.claim: The loss of CIB2 leads to profound hearing loss from birth in both humans and mice.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that the loss of CIB2 leads to profound hearing loss from birth in both humans and mice (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021; Seco et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The endogenous levels of CIB3 present in auditory hair cells are not sufficient to compensate for CIB2 in hearing.
claims.source: This suggests that the endogenous levels of CIB3 present in auditory hair cells are not sufficient to compensate for CIB2 in hearing.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of CIB2 causes hearing loss despite CIB3 expression.

claims.claim: Over-expression of CIB3 in mouse auditory outer hair cells can only partially compensate for the loss of CIB2 in MET.
claims.source: Prior work has also shown that over-expression of CIB3 in mouse auditory outer hair cells can only partially compensate for the loss of CIB2 in MET (Liang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Compared to auditory hair cells, the expression of CIB3 is several folds higher in vestibular end organs.
claims.source: While CIB2 is also present in vestibular hair cells, compared to auditory hair cells, the expression of CIB3 is several folds higher in vestibular end organs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by expression data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Endogenous levels of CIB3 can fully compensate for the loss of CIB2 in vestibular hair cells in mice.
claims.source: Indeed, our current data demonstrate that, unlike auditory hair cells, endogenous levels of CIB3 can fully compensate for the loss of CIB2 in vestibular hair cells in mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from vestibular hair cells in the current study.

claims.claim: Both CIB2 and CIB3 can play overlapping roles in MET function in the vestibular system in mice.
claims.source: Together our work on the vestibular system in mice highlights that both CIB2 and CIB3 can play overlapping roles in MET function.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from the vestibular system in mice.

claims.claim: In zebrafish, Cib3 can compensate for Cib2, but only in specific subsets of hair cells.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In vitro and in vivo functional data indicate that both TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins are needed for hair-cell MET.
claims.source: This is supported by structural data indicating multiple contact points between TMC and CIB proteins, simulation data predicting that CIB proteins stabilize TMC cytosolic domains and may enhance cation conduction, and in vitro and in vivo functional data indicating that both TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins are needed for hair-cell MET.

results.result: Cib2 and Cib3 are co-expressed in mouse vestibular hair cells, while Tmc1 is highly expressed and Tmc2 expression increases during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are supported by bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figures 1B-C. The expression patterns are clearly documented with appropriate controls and developmental time points.

results.result: CIB2 is indispensable for hearing in mice, while CIB3 knockout alone does not affect hearing.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by ABR measurements (Figure 2A-B), FM 1-43 dye uptake assays (Figure 2C), and hair cell degeneration analysis (Figure 2D). The data clearly show that Cib3KO/KO mice have normal hearing while Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice are profoundly deaf.

results.result: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice exhibit severe vestibular dysfunction including impaired VOR, circling behavior, poor rotarod performance, and head bobbing.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C60 are supported by comprehensive vestibular function tests shown in Figure 3, including VORd testing, OKR, open-field tests, rotarod performance, and head motion analysis. Multiple independent assays converge on the conclusion of severe vestibular deficits in double knockout mice.

results.result: CIB2 and CIB3 have compulsory but functionally redundant roles in mouse vestibular hair cell MET without causing hair cell degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by confocal imaging (Figure 4A) showing no hair cell loss and FM 1-43/FM 1-43 FX labeling experiments (Figures 4B-C) demonstrating complete loss of MET in double knockout mice while single mutants retain function. The data clearly establish functional redundancy.

results.result: In zebrafish, Cib2 is required for normal acoustic startle responses while Cib3 alone is not, but both are required together for complete auditory function.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by acoustic startle response data in Figure 5A showing significantly reduced responses in cib2 mutants (p=0.005), normal responses in cib3 mutants (p=0.36), and complete absence in double mutants. Statistical analysis is appropriate with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: Both Cib2 and Cib3 are required for normal MET in all zebrafish lateral-line hair cells, with Cib2 loss alone causing partial defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by FM 1-43 labeling data in Figure 5B-G showing significantly reduced labeling in cib2 mutants (37.5±6.9% vs 97.6±1.2% control, p<0.0001), normal labeling in cib3 mutants, and complete absence in double mutants. Quantification is rigorous with appropriate statistics.

results.result: Calcium imaging confirms that Cib2 and Cib3 are both required for normal mechanosensitive function in all zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing significantly fewer mechanosensitive cells in cib2 and double mutants (p<0.0001) with reduced response magnitudes, while cib3 mutants are normal. This provides independent validation of the FM 1-43 results.

results.result: Cib2 is specifically required for mechanosensitive function in zebrafish hair cells that express Tmc2a, based on hair cell orientation in lateral line and morphology in crista.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 are supported by FM 1-43 FX and FM 4-64 labeling experiments in Figure 6 showing that in cib2 mutants, residual functional hair cells are biased toward posterior flow-responsive cells (Tmc2b-expressing) in lateral line and tall cells (Tmc2b/Tmc1-expressing) in crista, while short cells (Tmc2a-expressing) fail to label. The inference about Tmc2a specificity is well-supported by the data pattern.

results.result: CIB proteins are clamped between TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 domains, as demonstrated by AlphaFold2 modeling and validated by NMR spectroscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C111 are supported by AF2 modeling (Figure 7A-B, supplements) and NMR data (Figure 7C, supplement 6) showing chemical shift perturbations upon sequential addition of TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT to labeled CIB2/3. The NMR data directly validate the clamp model and rule out direct CIB2-CIB3 interactions. The structural predictions are consistent across species.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations show that CIB proteins stabilize TMC N-terminal domains and maintain stable interactions over microsecond timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 are supported by MD simulation data in Figure 8 and supplements showing highly mobile TMC-NT in the absence of CIB proteins but stable conformations with CIB2/3 present. Anton 2 simulations confirm stability over 960 ns. BSA analysis suggests preferential TMC-CIB3 interactions. The computational methods are appropriate and well-described.

results.result: MD simulations with applied voltage demonstrate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels with conductance values consistent with MET channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C123, C129 are supported by MD simulations with applied voltage showing K+ permeation through TMC1/2 pores with conductance values up to ~138 pS in POPC bilayers, consistent with expected MET channel conductance when scaled appropriately. The simulations show almost exclusive K+ passage despite Cl- presence. Multiple conditions and membrane compositions were tested.

results.result: TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound, which may explain why CIB2 is essential for normal TMC1 function.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is supported by Anton 2 simulation data in Figure 8E showing a trend of higher conductance with CIB2. However, claim C124 is speculative ('may begin to explain') and the mechanistic link between increased conductance and essentiality is not directly demonstrated. Additional experimental validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: TMC2 simulations reveal a more closed state with lower conductance than TMC1, possibly due to intrinsic differences or incomplete opening without mechanical stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are partially supported by simulation data showing TMC2 conductance not exceeding ~64 pS. However, claims C127-C128 are explicitly speculative, and the authors acknowledge conflicting prior experimental data about TMC2 conductance. The limitation that the model may not represent a fully open state weakens the conclusions.

results.result: Endogenous CIB3 levels can fully compensate for CIB2 loss in mouse vestibular hair cells due to higher CIB3 expression compared to auditory hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C140-C141 are supported by FM 1-43 uptake data (Figure 1A) showing MET in Cib2KO/KO vestibular hair cells, expression data (Figure 1B-C) showing higher Cib3 expression in vestibular organs, and functional data (Figure 4) showing that only double knockout eliminates vestibular MET. The compensation mechanism is well-supported.

results.result: CIB2 loss causes profound hearing loss in humans and mice because endogenous CIB3 levels in auditory hair cells are insufficient for compensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 are supported by citations to prior research (C136, C138) and expression data from the current study (C139) showing several-fold higher CIB3 expression in vestibular vs auditory organs. The inference about insufficient compensation (C137) is logical given the hearing loss phenotype despite CIB3 presence.

results.result: The TMC-CIB functional relationship is conserved across vertebrates and possibly extends beyond vertebrates based on structural similarity to nematode proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C157 are supported by functional data from mouse and zebrafish (multiple figures), AF2 modeling showing conserved architecture across species (Figure 7 supplements), and structural similarity to nematode TMC-1/CALM-1 complex despite low sequence identity (36% and 51%). The conservation argument is well-supported by convergent evidence.

results.result: CIB2 is monomeric in solution while CIB3 shows dimeric behavior, but apparent CIB oligomerization in pull-down assays likely reflects TMC dimeric states rather than direct CIB-CIB interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C165 are supported by SEC data (Figure 7—figure supplement 5) showing single peak for CIB2 and two peaks for CIB3, NMR data ruling out direct CIB2-CIB3 interactions, and AF2 modeling showing each TMC monomer binds one CIB protein. The reconciliation of contradictory prior results through TMC oligomerization is logical and well-reasoned.

results.result: TMC1/2 proteins must function with CIB2/3 in normal hair-cell MET across sensory organs, hair-cell types, and species, supported by structural, computational, and in vivo data.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C180 represent the main conclusion synthesizing structural data (multiple contact points), simulation data (stabilization and enhanced conduction), and functional data (requirement for MET) from the entire manuscript. The convergent evidence from multiple independent approaches strongly supports this overarching conclusion.

results.result: CIB2 and CIB3 bind to TMC1 and TMC2, can form heteromeric complexes, interact with multiple TMC cytoplasmic domains simultaneously, and stabilize TMCs to form cation channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C5-C7 summarize the main findings validated throughout the manuscript by co-IP, NMR, AF2 modeling, MD simulations, and functional assays in mice and zebrafish. The evidence is comprehensive and convergent across multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Vestibular hair cells lacking CIB2 and CIB3 are not degenerated but have no detectable MET, providing strong genetic evidence for direct CIB-TMC functional relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 are supported by confocal imaging showing intact hair cells (Figure 4A) and FM 1-43 labeling showing no MET (Figures 4B-C) in double knockout mice. The parallel to Tmc1/Tmc2 double mutants (C134) strengthens the genetic argument. This is a key result establishing the functional requirement.

results.result: Various TMC/CIB complexes might explain tonotopic conductance variation, and Ca2+-dependent TMC-CIB interactions may have functional implications for adaptation, though these remain speculative.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C169, C172, C176 are explicitly speculative ('might explain', 'may have', 'might be') and acknowledged as such by the authors. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, these claims lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses for future work rather than established results.

results.result: CIB2 and CIB3 have functionally redundant roles in mouse vestibular hair cells. Single knockouts of either Cib2 or Cib3 show normal vestibular function and FM 1-43 dye uptake, but double knockout mice (Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO) exhibit severe vestibular deficits including impaired VOR, circling behavior, head bobbing, and complete loss of FM 1-43 uptake in vestibular hair cells without hair cell degeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'many of the basic results from the mouse have already been reported by other groups in Liang et al. (2021) and Wang et al. (2023),' indicating that the vestibular findings are confirmatory rather than novel. While the data are described as 'necessary and convincing' in some parts, the lack of novelty and overlap with prior publications reduces confidence in treating these as new contributions.

results.result: In zebrafish, Cib2 and Cib3 are both required for normal MET function in lateral-line hair cells. Loss of cib2 alone significantly reduces acoustic startle responses and FM 1-43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells, while cib3 mutants show normal responses. Double mutants (cib2;cib3) show complete absence of startle responses, FM 1-43 labeling, and mechanosensitive calcium responses in lateral-line hair cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'their demonstration of the importance of CIB2 and CIB3 in zebrafish hair cell function is novel' and note that 'the results largely coincide with what is seen in the mouse.' The zebrafish studies are regarded as 'necessary and convincing,' indicating reviewer acceptance of these findings as a significant contribution.

results.result: In zebrafish, Cib2 is specifically required for MET function in hair cell subtypes that express Tmc2a. In the lateral line, Cib2 is essential for anterior flow-responsive cells (which express Tmc2b and Tmc2a), while Cib3 can compensate in posterior flow-responsive cells (which express primarily Tmc2b). In the crista, Cib2 is required in both short cells (Tmc2a-expressing) and tall cells (Tmc2b/Tmc1-expressing), while Cib3 is required only in tall cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'cib2 is uniquely localized in and important for specific hair cell types in the neuromast and crista,' highlighting this as a novel and interesting finding. The specificity of Cib2 requirement for different hair cell subtypes is treated as a significant discovery that adds to understanding of the system.

results.result: AlphaFold 2 modeling predicts that CIB proteins simultaneously interact with at least two cytoplasmic domains of TMC1 and TMC2 (the N-terminus and IL1 domain), with CIB proteins 'clamped' between these domains. These predictions are validated by NMR spectroscopy showing simultaneous binding of TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 to CIB2 and CIB3, and are consistent with prior structural data including the crystal structure of TMC1-IL1 with CIB3.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that 'structural studies (AlphaFold 2 modeling, NMR structure determination, and molecular dynamics simulations) brings us closer to the structure of the mammalian TMCs' and that this work 'offers significant new findings.' The structural work is praised for supporting 'the assignment of the TMC pore to alpha helices 4-7' and for providing a framework to reconcile contradictory prior results.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations predict that CIB proteins structurally stabilize TMC cytoplasmic domains and that TMC1 and TMC2 form cation channels. Simulations show that TMC N-termini are highly mobile without CIB proteins but become stable when CIB2 or CIB3 are present. Ion permeation simulations demonstrate K+ conductance with values reaching up to ~138 pS for TMC1, consistent with expected MET channel conductance, and suggest that CIB2 binding may enhance TMC1 conductance.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the computational work as part of the manuscript, one reviewer notes that 'the grounding of the experimental and computational parts is different, and the firmness of conclusions, respectively, is not matched.' This suggests uncertainty about the strength of conclusions drawn from simulations compared to experimental data. The reviewer's comment that 'different components pull the emphasis in several directions with little cross-talk' indicates concerns about integration of computational and experimental findings.

results.result: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO double knockout mice are profoundly deaf with no ABR responses to click or tone burst stimuli, show no FM 1-43 dye uptake in auditory hair cells, and exhibit progressive degeneration of auditory hair cells, confirming that CIB2 is indispensable for hearing and MET function in auditory hair cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'many of the basic results from the mouse have already been reported by other groups in Liang et al. (2021) and Wang et al. (2023)' and describe parts of the paper as 'confirmatory studies' rather than novel findings. The auditory phenotype data are treated as replicating prior work rather than providing new insights.

results.result: Expression analysis shows that all four Cib family members are expressed in mouse inner ear tissues, but only Cib2 and Cib3 are expressed in immature and mature utricular hair cells (both type I and type II). Tmc1 is highly expressed in immature utricular hair cells while Tmc2 expression is low but increases during development, remaining below Tmc1 levels in mature hair cells.
results.evaluation: These expression data provide context for the functional studies and are not specifically critiqued by reviewers. The data support the rationale for focusing on CIB2 and CIB3 in vestibular hair cells and are treated as supporting evidence for the main findings.

results.result: The combined in vivo studies in mouse and zebrafish, along with structural modeling showing conserved architecture across species (including similarity to nematode TMC-1/CALM-1 complex), demonstrate that TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins form functionally conserved complexes that are integral to hair-cell MET across vertebrate species and sensory organs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the authors 'try to combine the three parts with the overarching theme of demonstrating that CIB2/3 play a functionally conserved role across species and hair cell types.' While one reviewer suggests the manuscript could be split, the conservation theme is treated as valid. The statement that the work provides 'a comprehensive look at the CIB family in hair cells' supports this integrative conclusion.
